title: How Ghana Growers Works
excerpt: A simple guide to how farmers, buyers, suppliers, and partners use Ghana Growers.
keyPoints: Farmers register their farm details and products.
Buyers browse supply or submit demand.
Suppliers register inputs, logistics, packaging, and services.
Ghana Growers reviews records before public visibility.

sections.heading: A practical network for agriculture
sections.body: Ghana Growers helps organize farmer profiles, marketplace listings, buyer requests, supplier services, and GG FarmMate tools in one place. The aim is simple: make it easier to know who produces what, where supply may be available, and how serious enquiries can be followed up.

sections.heading: What happens after registration
sections.body: Submitted farmer, buyer, and supplier records are reviewed before they are published. Complete records with clear products, location, contact details, and photos are easier to approve.

sections.heading: How connections happen
sections.body: Buyers and partners can request connections through Ghana Growers. This helps the platform track demand, follow up on serious enquiries, and reduce random contact that does not lead to useful trade.

title: Verification Process
excerpt: What Ghana Growers checks before showing verified status on farmers, suppliers, and buyer requests.
keyPoints: Verification checks contact details, profile completeness, and basic business information.
Verified status is shown publicly only after review.
Some profiles may need follow-up before publishing.
Verification does not guarantee price, quality, delivery, or payment.

sections.heading: What Ghana Growers reviews
sections.body: The review process looks at name, phone number, WhatsApp number, location, products or services, photos where available, and whether the record is complete enough for public use.

sections.heading: What verified means
sections.body: A verified profile has been reviewed by Ghana Growers. Buyers should still confirm availability, quality, quantity, delivery, and payment terms before making commitments.

sections.heading: How to prepare
sections.body: Submit a working phone number, WhatsApp number, region, district, main products or services, and a real photo or logo where possible.

title: How to Sell Produce Through Ghana Growers
excerpt: Steps farmers can take to make produce easier for buyers to discover and request.
keyPoints: Register with accurate location and contact details.
List crops, livestock, harvest periods, and quantities clearly.
Keep produce information practical and current.
Respond quickly when Ghana Growers follows up on buyer demand.

sections.heading: Start with a clear farmer profile
sections.body: Buyers need to understand who you are, where you farm, what you produce, and when you may be able to supply. A clear profile helps Ghana Growers match your farm with relevant buyer requests.

sections.heading: Share details buyers can use
sections.body: Useful information includes product name, expected quantity, harvest period, pickup or delivery arrangement, and whether supply is one-time, weekly, seasonal, or on request.

sections.heading: Keep communication simple
sections.body: When a buyer is interested, confirm the product, quantity, location, timing, and expected quality before discussing price or transport.

title: How Buyers Source Produce
excerpt: How buyers can find farmers, browse listings, submit demand, and request connections.
audience: Market traders, processors, restaurants, wholesalers, and institutions
keyPoints: Search farmer profiles and marketplace listings by product and region.
Submit buyer requests when supply is not listed.
Use clear quantities, timelines, and location details.
Confirm product quality and logistics before purchasing.

sections.heading: Browse first, request when needed
sections.body: Buyers can browse farmer profiles, supplier profiles, and marketplace listings. If the right product is not available yet, a buyer request helps Ghana Growers understand demand and look for matching supply.

sections.heading: Make your request specific
sections.body: Strong buyer requests include product, quantity, region, district, deadline, delivery preference, and any quality requirements.

sections.heading: Confirm before committing
sections.body: Always confirm availability, grade, packaging, pickup or delivery, and payment terms before making a buying decision.

title: Become a Supplier Guide
excerpt: What agricultural suppliers should prepare before joining Ghana Growers.
audience: Input dealers, logistics providers, packaging companies, consultants, and service providers
keyPoints: Share your supplier category and main products or services.
List the regions or districts you can serve.
Add a WhatsApp number and website if available.
Use clear service descriptions so farmers and buyers understand your offer.

sections.heading: Who should register
sections.body: Suppliers can include seed companies, fertilizer dealers, agrochemical shops, farm equipment providers, irrigation installers, packaging suppliers, logistics operators, storage providers, finance providers, and agricultural consultants.

sections.heading: What to include
sections.body: A useful supplier profile includes company name, contact person, category, products or services, coverage area, WhatsApp number, and a logo or service image when available.

sections.heading: How profiles help
sections.body: Supplier profiles help farmers and buyers discover services that support production, packaging, transport, storage, and market access.

title: Market Prices Explained
excerpt: How farmers and buyers should interpret market price information on Ghana Growers.
keyPoints: Prices are market intelligence, not guaranteed transaction prices.
Location, quality, packaging, and transport can change final price.
Trend direction can be as useful as the price itself.
Use price information alongside buyer demand and harvest timing.

sections.heading: Market prices are a guide
sections.body: Market prices help users understand direction and compare opportunities, but actual prices depend on quality, quantity, timing, packaging, transport, and buyer relationship.

sections.heading: How farmers can use price signals
sections.body: Farmers can use price signals to plan harvest timing, compare markets, and prepare for buyer conversations.

sections.heading: How buyers can use price signals
sections.body: Buyers can use market prices to estimate budgets and compare regional supply conditions before submitting requests.

title: Tomato Production: Field Checks Before Flowering
excerpt: Practical checks for tomato farmers before flowering and fruiting begin.
keyPoints: Check drainage after rain.
Look for early pest pressure under leaves.
Stake or support plants before heavy fruiting.
Avoid applying chemicals without confirming the issue.

sections.heading: Check the field after rain
sections.body: Tomatoes do not perform well in waterlogged soil. After heavy rain, check low areas of the field, clear blocked drains, and avoid leaving standing water around plant roots.

sections.heading: Inspect leaves early
sections.body: Look under leaves for small insects, yellowing, curling, spots, or chewing damage. Early checks help farmers act before a problem spreads across the field.

sections.heading: Prepare for fruiting
sections.body: Staking, pruning, and steady watering before fruiting can reduce losses. Farmers should confirm fertilizer and spray decisions with an extension officer or trusted agronomist when unsure.

title: Maize Leaves Turning Yellow: What to Check First
excerpt: A simple field guide for farmers who notice yellowing maize leaves.
keyPoints: Check whether yellowing starts on old or new leaves.
Look at soil moisture and drainage.
Check for pest damage or poor spacing.
Ask for expert confirmation before treating disease.

sections.heading: Start with the pattern
sections.body: If older leaves yellow first, the issue may be linked to nutrient stress. If newer leaves yellow, check for other stress signs. The pattern gives a useful clue, but it is not a final diagnosis.

sections.heading: Check water and roots
sections.body: Too much water, dry soil, poor drainage, or compacted soil can all affect maize growth. Farmers should check whether roots are healthy and whether water is sitting in the field.

sections.heading: Use Crop Doctor when unsure
sections.body: A clear photo can help Ghana Growers provide advisory guidance, but serious crop problems should be confirmed with an agricultural extension officer.

title: Simple Records for Small Poultry Flocks
excerpt: Record keeping that helps poultry keepers track feed, mortality, eggs, and sales.
keyPoints: Track feed purchases and daily use.
Record egg collection and bird losses.
Watch changes in water intake and behaviour.
Use records before making buying or selling decisions.

sections.heading: Why records matter
sections.body: Small poultry farmers can lose money without noticing where costs are rising. Simple records help track feed, eggs, mortality, medicine, and sales.

sections.heading: What to write down
sections.body: Record date, feed quantity, eggs collected, birds lost, medicine used, and sales. Even a notebook can help farmers see patterns.

sections.heading: Use records for buyer conversations
sections.body: If a buyer asks for regular supply, records help the farmer know what quantity can be supplied and how often.

title: Starting a Backyard Vegetable Garden
excerpt: A practical guide for growing vegetables at home with limited space.
keyPoints: Choose a sunny place with access to water.
Start with vegetables you cook often.
Use compost or well-prepared soil.
Water in the morning or late afternoon.

sections.heading: Start small
sections.body: A small garden is easier to manage than a large one. Begin with crops such as pepper, tomato, okra, kontomire, spring onion, or garden eggs depending on your space.

sections.heading: Prepare the soil
sections.body: Mix soil with compost or well-rotted organic matter. Avoid planting in soil that holds too much water or dries out too quickly.

sections.heading: Keep checking the plants
sections.body: Home gardens need regular observation. Check leaves, soil moisture, weeds, and pest signs before problems become serious.

title: Rainy Season Farm Checklist
excerpt: A short checklist for preparing fields, drainage, seed, and labour before the rains.
keyPoints: Prepare drainage before heavy rain.
Check seed quality before planting.
Plan labour early.
Watch weather updates before spraying.

sections.heading: Prepare before the field gets busy
sections.body: Before the main rains, farmers should check drainage, seed availability, tools, labour, and field access. Waiting until the rains are heavy can delay planting.

sections.heading: Protect soil and young crops
sections.body: Heavy rain can wash away soil or damage young plants. Good spacing, drainage, and mulching where suitable can help reduce stress.

sections.heading: Use weather before field work
sections.body: Check rain chance before spraying, fertilizer application, or harvest work. GG FarmMate weather guidance can help farmers plan daily tasks.

title: Video Guide: How to Use Crop Doctor
excerpt: A short video guide placeholder for farmers learning how to upload crop photos for advisory guidance.
keyPoints: Take a clear photo of the affected leaf or plant.
Use good light and avoid blurry photos.
Read results as guidance, not final diagnosis.
Confirm serious problems with an extension officer.

sections.heading: What the video will cover
sections.body: This guide will show farmers how to take a clear crop photo, upload it to Crop Doctor, read the result, and decide when to ask for expert confirmation.

sections.heading: Important reminder
sections.body: Crop Doctor provides advisory guidance only. Farmers should confirm serious disease, pest, or chemical decisions with a qualified agricultural extension officer.
